full_text:
Stanford just reinvented text generation.

(it’s neither autoregressive nor diffusion)

Autoregressive LLMs generate one token at a time. Longer answers require longer chains of sequential predictions.

Diffusion LLMs generate many tokens in parallel, but still need repeated refinement passes. Each pass processes the full sequence, and quality drops quickly when you cut the passes.

Stanford researchers proposed another approach, Next-Concept Modeling (NCM). It generates text from coarse structure to fine detail in roughly a dozen passes.

First, a tokenizer learns to represent text as layers of compressed information. Early layers capture broad structure, while later layers add details the earlier ones missed.

A transformer then learns to generate these layers in order, predicting everything within each layer simultaneously. A decoder converts the completed representation into text.

The advantage is that early layers are tiny. Generation needs fewer passes, and those early passes process much less information.

You can see this in the team’s translation example. Early layers produce rough, repetitive text, which later layers refine into a clean translation.

In the researchers’ tests, NCM generated text 10–31× faster than strong diffusion baselines, with comparable or better benchmark scores. On LM1B and OpenWebText, it also used roughly 4–5× fewer training tokens, including tokenizer training.

That speed can also improve quality. Generating several candidates and selecting one based on agreement outperformed diffusion baselines at the same sampling time budget.

The limits matter. Scaling experiments reach 725M parameters, tasks use separate tokenizers, and the release includes evaluation code and checkpoints without a training pipeline.

Some evaluations also use repetition penalties during final decoding, without additional model calls.

NCM shows that parallel generation can work by building increasingly detailed representations. Whether those gains hold at general-purpose LLM scale remains open.

- Paper: https://t.co/G5v0TVpzwj

JUST IN: 🇮🇩Indonesia’s stock market wiped out $60,000,000,000 today, its worst day in 28 years.

The Jakarta Composite closed down 11.57% at 5,185, a level not seen in almost 26 years.

The last bigger daily drop came during the 1998 Asian financial crisis, when a collapsing rupiah drove up foreign debt costs and deepened a banking crisis.

The index is now down about 40% this year.

The fall comes amid MSCI proposing to strip Indonesia of emerging-market status over opaque ownership, suspected coordinated trading and weak enforcement.

That could force funds tracking its global indices to sell Indonesian stocks.

UBS estimates around $4 BILLION in passive outflows, with active investors potentially withdrawing another $15 BILLION.

The downgrade is still pending, with a final decision due by June 2027.

The rout comes as South Korea’s KOSPI fell -14.46% this week, its worst week since the 2008 financial crisis.

BREAKING: Bali has run out of fuel, with hours-long queues outside gas stations since Sunday and attendants posting signs reading "Sorry, no fuel available." Shortages are now hitting at least 11 Indonesian provinces.

Waiting times reached 2 to 3 hours in West Sumatra, and diesel queues ran about a kilometre on the Merak-Tangerang highway in Banten. Diesel or Pertalite sold out in Aceh, Riau, West Kalimantan, South Sulawesi, North Sulawesi and Yogyakarta.

Fuel tenders now attract few participants, per Indonesia's oil and gas director general, forcing the government to seek supplies directly from countries with surplus stocks at higher prices. Indonesia lost 25% of its fuel import sources after the Iran war began.

Bali is now preparing to restrict subsidised fuel sales to the top income decile.

Everyone knows I've been bearish on specific parts of the AI trade. Just search my profile, I've been saying it for months.

To be clear, I'm not bearish on AI. I'm bearish on bad business models being priced like good AI companies.

If you break the trade down to first principles, there are two very different categories in the basket right now:

Infrastructure that has to exist regardless of who wins

$ASML - There is literally no alternative. If you want to make an advanced chip, you go through them. It's a monopoly plain and simple.

$SITM - Nobody talks about it, but timing is in every single piece of hardware. It's the lowest level, most defensible layer. It doesn’t matter what happens with data centers, technology is moving towards MEMS with robotics, space, military, communications, ect. Forward P/E in mid 30s now, i think it’s one of the best buys in the market despite throwing the baby out with the bath water. 

$NBIS - I am slightly skeptical on the path to profitability as well as valuation but it’s hard to argue that they’re not the best infra play . Owns the data centers, owns the software layer, has a backlog of actual enterprise clients who can't get capacity elsewhere. They have pricing power because they built something hard to build.

Those companies work even if capex slows down 20%. They work if the cycle pauses.

Then you have $CRWV and some other names including the frontier models.

This is the problem with the entire basket. CoreWeave is a neocloud that rents depreciating assets with leverage. $2.5B+ in quarterly revenue, $104B in backlog, but $21-25B in debt today with up to $68B in potential future obligations, a $35-39B capex plan for 2026 alone, deeply negative free cash flow (-$4.7B last quarter on $7.7B capex), and interest expense ($640M in Q2, guided $860-940M in Q3) growing faster than operating income. Adjusted operating income was $128M in Q2 on double the revenue vs $200M a year ago.

And the structure is circular. Nvidia owns ∼7% of CoreWeave, invested $2B in equity in January 2026, CoreWeave uses that money to buy Nvidia chips, Nvidia books it as revenue, and Nvidia contractually backstops $6.3B of unsold CoreWeave capacity through 2032. It's demand pulled forward with debt.

When rates stay higher, or when one contract slips, that entire leverage loop unwinds. And because passive flows and retail traders own AI as a *basket* through ETFs and thematic funds, the unwind doesn't just hit CRWV. It hits SITM, NBIS, ASML, NVDA. All of it gets sold together.

That's the flaw in the current market. We're letting the weakest business model set the multiple for the strongest companies.

Outside of the direct AI trade: the software and distribution layers of $RDDT, $TEM and $LMND will continue to perform. $ODD is likely seen as the biggest hedge for me at least and it is why I have been buying heavily the past month. 

I'm not short AI. In the next phase, the market will stop buying "AI" and start buying actual infrastructure. Have no clue how aggressive this will get but I think its exactly what needs to happen.
